questions.explanation: Correct Answer: E. Educational Objective: This patient presents with the acute onset of confusion, hyperthermia, and muscle rigidity 2 weeks after beginning antipsychotic use. This presentation is consistent with neuroleptic malignant syndrome (NMS). Evaluation: NMS is a life-threatening condition associated with the antagonism of dopamine that presents with altered mental status, muscle rigidity, hyperthermia, and autonomic dysfunction. Common causative agents are antipsychotics (especially high-potency antipsychotics such as haloperidol as in this case) and antidopaminergic nausea medications. Definition: NMS results from blockade of dopamine within several pathways. Rigidity results from dopamine antagonism in the nigrostriatal pathway, while autonomic dysfunction and hyperthermia may result from dopamine antagonism in the hypothalamus. Characteristic laboratory abnormalities include leukocytosis and increased serum creatine kinase, lactate dehydrogenase, and alkaline phosphatase (due to prolonged muscle rigidity and consequent myolysis). Prevention: NMS can sometimes be prevented by avoiding combining antidopaminergic agents and high doses of high-potency antipsychotics. Treatment: Treatment is supportive and includes discontinuation of the offending medication, hydration, cooling blankets, and benzodiazepines if needed for agitation. Dantrolene is potentially beneficial. Differential: This patient presents with rigidity, autonomic instability, and confusion 2 weeks after initiating high-potency antipsychotic therapy, a presentation consistent with NMS. Rigidity is a defining feature of NMS, whereas clonus is the key feature of the similarly presenting serotonin syndrome. Incorrect Answers: A, B, C, and D. Choice A: Endocrinopathy is incorrect. Though the patient has a family history of thyroid disease and thyroid storm can present with confusion and hyperthermia, muscle rigidity would be atypical. As well, lid lag and tremors are common in thyroid storm, and tachycardia would be more severe than in this patient. Choice B: Heat stroke is incorrect. Heat stroke presents with hyperthermia, tachycardia, tachypnea, and altered mental status. However, other examination findings commonly include flushed, dry skin and manifestations of coagulopathy such as ecchymosis. As well, increased muscle tone would be atypical. Choice C: Malignant hyperthermia is incorrect. Malignant hyperthermia is caused by a genetic defect in the ryanodine receptor and presents with muscle rigidity, tachycardia, fever, lactic acidosis, and hypercarbia when the patient is exposed to succinylcholine or volatile anesthetics. While the presentation is similar to NMS, this patient has not been exposed to agents that trigger malignant hyperthermia, making this a less likely cause of his symptoms. Choice D: Myocardial ischemia is incorrect. Hyperthermia and muscle rigidity following antipsychotic use are atypical of myocardial ischemia.

Educational Objective: The most likely diagnosis in this patient with positional episodes of dizziness associated with provokable nystagmus is benign paroxysmal positional vertigo (BPPV). The most appropriate initial step in management of this pathology is an otolith repositioning maneuver. Evaluation: Patients with BPPV typically report symptoms of intensive, brief episodes of vertigo that occur after changes in position (such as rolling over) and are accompanied by visual disturbances (due to nystagmus), nausea, and vomiting. Definition: BPPV occurs when an otolith becomes dislodged and enters the semicircular canal. Changes in head posture then cause the malpositioned otolith to move within the semicircular canal, stimulating abnormal movements in endolymph, and causing a sensation of vertigo. Positional oculovestibular testing, such as the Dix-Hallpike test (described in this case), allows the examiner to reproduce the patient’s symptoms by repositioning the otolith. Prevention: There is no preventative measure for benign positional vertigo. Treatment: Further positional maneuvers, such as the Epley maneuver, can be used to reposition the otolith to its proper position within the utricle. Patients with refractory symptoms may benefit from medical management including scopolamine or meclizine. Differential: This patient’s episodic vertigo with head positioning and lack of additional neurologic symptoms is consistent with BPPV, the treatment for which is otolith repositioning. No further specific diagnostic steps are needed at this time, and the first-line therapy should be attempted before adjunctive options. Incorrect Answers: A, B, C, and D. Choice A: High-dose prednisone therapy is incorrect. High-dose prednisone therapy is occasionally used in the treatment of vestibular neuritis, caused by inflammation of the vestibulocochlear nerve. Vestibular neuritis presents with persistent (rather than transient) vertigo associated with spontaneous nystagmus, symptoms that are not seen in this patient. Choice B: Hydrochlorothiazide therapy is incorrect. Hydrochlorothiazide is a diuretic that can be used as a preventative treatment in Meniere disease. Vertigo associated with Meniere disease often lasts for prolonged periods of time and may also present with hearing loss or tinnitus. This patient has short periods of vertigo with no associated auditory symptoms, making Meniere disease unlikely. Choice C: Meclizine therapy is incorrect. Meclizine is an antihistamine used in the treatment of vertigo, motion sickness, and nausea. Meclizine may be used as a second-line therapy in patients who do not find relief with otolith repositioning maneuvers. Choice D: MR angiography is incorrect. MR angiography can be used to evaluate the cerebral vasculature and may be indicated if there is concern for a cerebellar or brain stem infarct. Vertigo associated with these types of strokes are typically sudden in onset, persistent, and associated with other neurologic symptoms, of which this patient has none.

Educational Objective: This young adult female patient presents with a recently increased BMI and signs of increased intracranial pressure, including headaches, visual disturbances, papilledema, and cranial nerve (lateral rectus) palsy; the most likely diagnosis is idiopathic intracranial hypertension. Evaluation: Idiopathic intracranial hypertension presents with throbbing headaches, visual disturbances (including but not limited to blurry vision, loss of vision, and scotomata), and cranial nerve dysfunction (especially the abducens nerve–lateral rectus palsy). Evaluation typically shows papilledema and may show increased opening pressure on lumbar puncture with otherwise normal cerebrospinal fluid. Definition: Idiopathic intracranial hypertension is characterized by increased intracranial pressure without an identifiable mass lesion or hydrocephalus. It most commonly affects female patients age 16 to 49 years who have an increased BMI and take medications such as oral contraceptives, danazol, and vitamin A derivatives. Increased pressure leads to optic nerve swelling (papilledema), which can cause visual symptoms and, if untreated, permanent vision loss. Lateral rectus palsy is common, resulting in diplopia. Neuroimaging may be normal, though it is required to exclude secondary causes before diagnosis. Prevention: Weight management and avoidance of precipitating medications may decrease risk. Treatment: Minorly symptomatic patients with normal vision require monitoring only. Patients with abnormal vision and more severe symptom presentations require treatment through risk factor modification (eg, weight loss), and initial pharmacotherapy with carbonic anhydrase inhibitors (eg, acetazolamide) to decrease cerebrospinal fluid production. Severe or vision-threatening cases may require surgical intervention. Differential: The presence of objective findings, such as papilledema, diplopia, and cranial nerve palsy and subjective findings, like recent weight gain and oral contraceptive use, distinguishes this case from migraines or cluster headaches. Incorrect Answers: A, C, D, and E. Choice A: Cluster headache is incorrect. Cluster headaches present with unilateral periorbital pain and autonomic symptoms (lacrimation, nasal congestion), not bilateral symptoms, papilledema, or cranial nerve palsy. Cluster headaches often occur in a cyclic/recurrent pattern over days, weeks, or times of the day or year, and more often occur in patients who are biologically male. Choice C: Migraine with aura is incorrect. Although migraines can cause throbbing headaches and visual symptoms, migraines do not cause papilledema or cranial nerve palsies. Neurologic examination is typically normal in simple migraines as well. Choice D: Retinal migraine is incorrect. Retinal migraine is rare. Retinal migraine causes transient monocular vision disturbance rather than bilateral visual change and is not associated with signs of increased intracranial pressure. Papilledema is specific for increased intracranial pressure or obstruction of fluid outflow along the optic nerve. Choice E: Temporal arteritis is incorrect. Temporal arteritis is rare in younger persons. It generally occurs in patients older than 50 years and presents with jaw claudication, scalp tenderness, and increased inflammatory markers, which are not seen in this 25-year-old woman.

questions.explanation: Correct Answer: B. Educational Objective: This patient presents with acute-onset, focal neurologic deficits which raise concern for stroke. The most appropriate next step in management is emergent evaluation with noncontrast CT scan of the head to detect potential intracranial hemorrhage and differentiate ischemic from hemorrhagic stroke. Evaluation: Patients with acute stroke present with acute focal neurologic deficits such as unilateral weakness, aphasia, or dysarthria, as seen in this patient. Initial evaluation includes emergent noncontrast CT scan of the head to determine initial care and determine type of stroke. If hemorrhagic stroke is ruled out, CT angiography is required prior to initiation of therapies such as thrombolytics and thrombectomy. Definition: Strokes result from ischemic (most, 80% to 85%) or hemorrhagic (15% to 20%) loss of blood flow. Carotid endarterectomy carries a risk for both thromboembolic stroke and reperfusion-related intracerebral hemorrhage, particularly within the first few days following surgery. Because management differs for each type of stroke, (anticoagulation or thrombolysis for ischemic stroke versus blood pressure control and reverse of anticoagulation for hemorrhagic stroke), imaging is required before treatment. CT scan is the fastest and most effective initial modality for detection of acute hemorrhage or assessment of large vessel occlusion. Prevention: Prevention of intracranial hemorrhage includes protection against head trauma and management of vascular risk factors. Hypertension increases the risk for hemorrhagic transformation or intracerebral bleeding along with thrombotic stroke. Perioperative blood pressure control after carotid endarterectomy decreases the risk for reperfusion syndrome and intracerebral hemorrhage. Antiplatelet therapy helps prevent thromboembolic complications. Treatment: Treatment depends on imaging findings: ischemic stroke may be treated with thrombolytics, if eligible and safe in the postoperative period; hemorrhagic stroke requires blood pressure control and supportive care. Differential: In this patient with acute neurologic deficits shortly after carotid surgery, both ischemic and hemorrhagic stroke are possible. Fast, diagnostic imaging is critical. Incorrect Answers: A, C, D, and E. Choice A: Cerebral angiography is incorrect. Although conventional angiography can identify vascular occlusions and hemorrhage, it is not the most appropriate initial test to evaluate for acute stroke. A CT scan can first rule out hemorrhage or large vessel occlusion and is not as time consuming or invasive as conventional angiography, nor does CT scan require intra-arterial contrast administration. Choice C: Echocardiography is incorrect. Echocardiography is used to evaluate cardiac sources of emboli; it is not used in the emergent evaluation of acute focal neurologic deficits. Echocardiography would be appropriate after the initial diagnostic and therapeutic phase of a stroke to assess cardioembolic sources. Choice D: Intravenous heparin therapy is incorrect. Anticoagulation should not be started until hemorrhagic stroke has been excluded by imaging, as it could worsen bleeding. Educational Objective: This patient most likely has myasthenia gravis, which causes fluctuating fatigable weakness that worsens with use and is most commonly due to antibodies against postsynaptic acetylcholine receptors at the neuromuscular junction. Evaluation: This patient has fluctuating bulbar symptoms with dysphagia, dysarthria, hypernasal speech, and arm weakness that worsen later in the day, consistent with fatigable weakness from myasthenia gravis. Definition: Myasthenia gravis is an autoimmune disorder of the neuromuscular junction caused most commonly by IgG antibodies against postsynaptic acetylcholine receptors. These antibodies impair neuromuscular transmission by blocking receptor function, accelerating receptor degradation, and activating complement-mediated damage to the postsynaptic membrane. Symptoms include fluctuating weakness involving ocular, bulbar, respiratory, and proximal limb muscles, often worsening with repeated use and improving with rest. Bulbar involvement can cause dysphagia, dysarthria, nasal speech, and weight loss due to impaired oral intake. Prevention: There is no primary prevention but recognizing fatigable bulbar or respiratory symptoms early helps prevent aspiration and myasthenic crisis. Avoidance of exacerbating medications, infections, and physiologic stressors can decrease worsening symptoms in diagnosed patients. Treatment: Treatment includes acetylcholinesterase inhibitors for symptomatic control and immunosuppressive therapy for disease modification. Severe bulbar or respiratory involvement requires urgent evaluation and may require intravenous immune globulin or plasma exchange. Differential: Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome causes proximal weakness that improves with repeated use and is associated with antibodies against presynaptic voltage-gated calcium channels. Botulism causes descending weakness with autonomic symptoms due to impaired acetylcholine release from the presynaptic terminal. Incorrect Answers: B, C, D, E, and F. Choice B: Presynaptic acetylcholine receptor is incorrect. Acetylcholine receptors are located on the postsynaptic muscle membrane, not the presynaptic nerve terminal. Voltage-gated calcium channels relevant to neuromuscular transmission are located presynaptically and regulate acetylcholine release. Choice F: Presynaptic voltage-gated calcium ion channel is incorrect. Antibodies to these channels cause Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome, which presents with proximal weakness that improves with repeated activity.

questions.explanation: Correct Answer: C. Educational Objective: Hepatic encephalopathy is a reversible condition caused by impaired hepatic detoxification leading to accumulation of ammonia. Patients with chronic liver disease who develop acute confusion, lethargy, and asterixis, as in this case, should be evaluated promptly for this condition. Evaluation: Hepatic encephalopathy typically presents in patients with underlying liver dysfunction as acute or subacute confusion, altered level of consciousness, and neurologic findings such as tremor or asterixis. It is diagnosed clinically in the setting of liver disease and may be supported by increased ammonia concentrations. Definition: Hepatic encephalopathy occurs when the liver is unable to adequately detoxify ammonia and nitrogenous waste products, allowing them to accumulate and cross the blood-brain barrier, leading to cerebral edema and altered mental status. Precipitants include infection, gastrointestinal bleeding, dehydration, electrolyte imbalances, and increased protein consumption. Chronic alcohol use is a risk factor because of its role in causing cirrhosis and liver dysfunction. Laboratory findings reflect impaired hepatic synthetic function (increased INR, low albumin) and hepatocellular injury (increased AST and ALT), as seen in this patient. Prevention: Prevention involves managing chronic liver disease and avoiding precipitating factors such as infections, constipation, and excessive dietary protein. Medications like lactulose can also decrease ammonia concentrations. Treatment: Treatment includes lactulose to decrease ammonia absorption in the gut and rifaximin to decrease ammonia-producing gut bacteria. Addressing precipitating factors is essential. Differential: In this patient with alcohol use disorder, abnormal liver function tests, ascites, and acute confusion, hepatic encephalopathy is the most likely cause. The presence of tremor and wide-based gait in the setting of liver dysfunction supports this diagnosis. Incorrect Answers: A, B, D, and E. Choice A: Alcohol-induced hallucinosis is incorrect. Alcohol-induced hallucinosis typically presents with auditory hallucinations in a patient who is otherwise alert and oriented, without the global confusion and lethargy seen in this patient. Alcohol-induced hallucinosis is often a consequence of acute alcohol withdrawal, occurring within 24 to 72 hours after the most recent drink. Choice B: Cerebellar hemorrhage is incorrect. Although a wide-based gait can be seen with cerebellar lesions, cerebellar hemorrhage presents with acute headache, vomiting, and focal neurologic deficits rather than progressive confusion in the setting of liver failure. This patient has risk factors for cerebellar hemorrhage but lacks the associated clinical features. Choice D: Hepatocerebral degeneration is incorrect. Hepatocerebral degeneration is a chronic, irreversible neurologic complication of long-standing liver disease, presenting with movement disorders, not acute changes in mental status over 3 days. Choice E: Manganese toxicity is incorrect. Manganese toxicity results from overexposure (often in metal workers, miners, or welders) and causes parkinsonian symptoms. It presents chronically, and there may be associated psychiatric symptoms such as hallucinations or emotional lability. This patient’s presentation is acute, and she has had no clear exposure to manganese.

questions.explanation: Correct Answer: F. Educational Objective: A deficiency of vitamin B12 (cobalamin) is the most likely cause of these findings. Vitamin B12 deficiency causes megaloblastic anemia, along with neurologic deficits caused by impaired myelin synthesis. The presence of neurologic symptoms distinguishes vitamin B12 deficiency from other causes of macrocytic anemia. Evaluation: Vitamin B12 deficiency presents with fatigue, macrocytic anemia, and neurologic findings such as paresthesia, decreased vibration sense, and weakness. Diagnosis is suggested by increased mean corpuscular volume and hypersegmented neutrophils on smear and is confirmed with low serum vitamin B12 concentrations. Definition: Vitamin B12 deficiency leads to impaired DNA synthesis, resulting in megaloblastic anemia. It also leads to demyelination of the dorsal columns and lateral corticospinal tracts, leading to neurologic deficits. Common causes include pernicious anemia, malabsorption, gastric surgery, malnutrition, and a vegan diet. Neurologic manifestations include peripheral neuropathy, ataxia, and decreased proprioception and vibration sense. Neurologic deficits may be irreversible if not treated promptly. Prevention: Prevention includes adequate dietary intake of vitamin B12 (cyanocobalamin) and supplementation in at-risk populations such as older individuals and those with malabsorption or vegan diets. Patients with pernicious anemia require lifelong supplementation. Treatment: Treatment consists of cyanocobalamin replacement, typically via intramuscular injections in cases of malabsorption. Early treatment can reverse hematologic abnormalities and may improve neurologic symptoms. Differential: In this patient with macrocytic anemia and neurologic deficits (paresthesias and decreased vibration sense), vitamin B12 deficiency is the most likely cause. The neurologic findings distinguish it from other causes of macrocytic anemia, such as folic acid deficiency, which causes anemia without neurologic involvement. Incorrect Answers: A, B, C, D, E, G, and H. Choice A: Folic acid is incorrect. Folic acid deficiency causes megaloblastic anemia with hypersegmented neutrophils; however, folic acid deficiency does not cause neurologic symptoms. Folic acid deficiency is more common in individuals with chronic alcohol use disorder. Choice B: Niacin is incorrect. Niacin deficiency causes pellagra, which presents with dermatitis, diarrhea, and dementia, not macrocytic anemia with neurologic deficits. Niacin deficiency does not have known hematologic manifestations. Choice C: Vitamin A is incorrect. Vitamin A deficiency leads to night blindness and xerophthalmia, not anemia or neuropathy. Choice D: Vitamin B1 (thiamine) is incorrect. Thiamine deficiency causes beriberi and Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome. Neither of these conditions is accompanied by megaloblastic anemia. Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome presents with neurologic symptoms including confusion, ophthalmoplegia, ataxia, confabulation, and hallucinations. Choice E: Vitamin B2 (riboflavin) is incorrect. Riboflavin deficiency causes cheilosis and glossitis, not macrocytic anemia or neuropathy. Choice G: Vitamin C is incorrect. Vitamin C deficiency causes scurvy, characterized by bleeding gums and poor wound healing, and abnormal hair growth, not macrocytic anemia with neurologic deficits. Choice H: Vitamin E is incorrect. Vitamin E deficiency can cause neurologic symptoms but does not cause megaloblastic anemia with hypersegmented neutrophils.

questions.explanation: Correct Answer: E. Educational Objective: The most likely diagnosis in this patient with early postural instability with falls, vertical gaze palsy, and axial rigidity with neck extension, is progressive supranuclear palsy (PSP). Evaluation: PSP varies in presentation early in the disease and has several phenotypes in patients with tau pathology at autopsy. This patient has early gait instability, difficulty with downward gaze, frequent falls, and axial rigidity with neck extension, which localize to a brain stem neurodegenerative process. This presentation is consistent with the classic phenotype of PSP, (the Richardson phenotype) known for disordered gait, postural instability, and falls. Definition: PSP is a neurodegenerative tauopathy characterized by accumulation of neurofibrillary tangles in brain stem nuclei and basal ganglia. It presents with vertical gaze palsy, especially impaired downward gaze, early postural instability with frequent falls, axial rigidity, and a stiff, extended neck posture. Cognitive impairment and bradykinesia may also occur, but response to dopaminergic therapy is typically poor. The disease progresses rapidly and is associated with a shortened survival compared to other Parkinsonian syndromes. Prevention: There are no known preventive strategies for PSP. Early recognition is important for safety planning and supportive care. Treatment: Management is supportive and focuses on fall prevention, physical therapy, and speech therapy for dysphagia. There are no pharmacotherapies that provide significant symptomatic benefits; medications used in Parkinson disease are generally ineffective. Differential: Parkinson disease presents with resting tremor, bradykinesia, and stooped posture with flexion rather than extension, and typically responds to levodopa. Huntington disease presents with choreiform movements and psychiatric symptoms rather than rigidity and gaze palsy. Incorrect Answers: A, B, C, and D. Choice A: Dementia, Alzheimer type is incorrect. Dementia, Alzheimer type presents with progressive memory loss and cortical atrophy rather than early gait instability and gaze palsy. Choice B: Huntington disease is incorrect. Huntington disease presents with chorea, psychiatric changes, and cognitive decline, not axial rigidity and gaze palsy. Choice C: Idiopathic torsion dystonia is incorrect. Idiopathic torsion dystonia presents with sustained muscle contractions and abnormal postures, not progressive gaze palsy and falls. Choice D: Parkinson disease is incorrect. Parkinson disease presents with resting tremor, bradykinesia, and stooped posture with flexion rather than neck extension and gaze palsy.

questions.explanation: Correct Answer: I. Educational Objective: The most likely diagnosis for this patient is temporal lobe glioma, which can cause contralateral superior homonymous quadrantanopia by compressing Meyer loop fibers and may present with headache, papilledema, and focal neurologic deficits from increased intracranial pressure. Educational Objective: This patient has a large blood pressure discrepancy between arms, absent pulses in the left upper extremity, and reversal of flow in the left vertebral artery. questions.explanation: Correct Answer: A. Educational Objective: Patients without eligible surrogate decision-makers should be assigned a court-appointed guardian for medical decisions. Organ donation is a medical decision that requires informed consent. Key Concept: Organ donation requires informed consent from a patient or, if the patient cannot demonstrate decision-making capacity, a surrogate decision-maker. Explanation: Legally, surrogate decision-making should follow this order: 1) Advance directives or other written documentation of the patient’s wishes, 2) durable power of attorney, 3) spouse, 4) adult children, 5) parents, 6) adult siblings, and 7) other adult relatives. In patients without an eligible surrogate, a court-appointed guardian is required. Medical teams can submit a guardianship application in these unique scenarios. Differential: Physicians can only provide surrogate informed consent when no other surrogate decision-maker is available and a delay in the decision would result in danger to life or limb, which is not the case with this patient. Hospital ethics panels can help resolve ethical dilemmas or mediate conflicts, but do not possess the authority to provide informed consent. Minors are not legally permitted to serve as surrogate decision makers, making it necessary for the informed consent in this case to come from a court-appointed guardian rather than the patient’s younger sister. Educational Objective: Neurocardiogenic (vasovagal) syncope, also known as fainting, is the most common cause of transient loss of consciousness and is typically triggered by prolonged standing, emotional stress, or heat exposure. It is characterized by a transient reflex causing hypotension and bradycardia, leading to decreased cerebral perfusion. Evaluation: Patients experiencing neurocardiogenic syncope often report fainting after prolonged standing or emotional stress, with brief loss of consciousness and rapid recovery without postictal confusion. Diagnosis is clinical, supported by a normal physical examination and ECG, and absence of concerning cardiac or neurologic findings. Patients generally report seconds to minutes of prodrome including nausea, flushing, sweating, tunnel vision, hearing a buzzing or ringing sound, and light-headedness before actual loss of consciousness. Definition: Neurocardiogenic syncope results from an exaggerated autonomic reflex that leads to sudden vasodilation and/or bradycardia. This reflex is often triggered by venous pooling (eg, prolonged standing) or increased emotions. The decreased preload along with vasodilation and bradycardia decreases cerebral perfusion. Neurocardiogenic syncope is common in otherwise healthy individuals and does not indicate underlying structural heart disease. Recovery is typically rapid and complete once the patient is supine. Prevention: Prevention includes avoiding known triggers, such as prolonged standing, and maintaining adequate hydration. Physical counterpressure maneuvers (eg, leg crossing) may help abort episodes. Treatment: Treatment is conservative, including reassurance and education. In recurrent cases, increased salt and fluid intake or medications may be considered. Differential: In this healthy patient who fainted while standing in a choir loft with rapid recovery and normal ECG, vasovagal syncope is the most likely cause of this patient's loss of consciousness. The lack of cardiac abnormalities or neurologic deficits helps distinguish it from arrhythmias or neurologic causes. Incorrect Answers: A, B, D, E, F, and G. Choice A: Autonomic neuropathy is incorrect. Autonomic neuropathy typically occurs in patients with longstanding diabetes mellitus and causes orthostatic hypotension rather than an isolated syncopal episode. Choice B: Hypoglycemia is incorrect. Hypoglycemia usually presents with adrenergic symptoms (eg, sweating, tremor) and altered mental status rather than a brief syncopal episode with rapid recovery in a healthy individual. Hypoglycemia in nonfasting patients without endocrinopathies or metabolic disease or on certain medications is uncommon. Choice D: Sick sinus syndrome is incorrect. Sick sinus syndrome typically occurs in older adults and is associated with abnormal ECG findings such as sinus bradycardia or pauses, which are not present here. This patient has a normal ventricular rate on ECG. Choice E: Third-degree atrioventricular block is incorrect. Complete (third degree atrioventricular) heart block presents with bradycardia and is diagnosed by abnormal ECG findings including a ventricular rate of 30–45/min and atrioventricular dissociation. Patients are often hypotensive and present with recurrent syncope. Choice F: Transient ischemic attack is incorrect. Transient ischemic attacks do not typically cause loss of consciousness and instead present with focal neurologic deficits that resolve within 24 hours. Transient ischemic attack causing loss of consciousness would be rare and involve the brain stem. Choice G: Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome is incorrect. Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome is associated with tachyarrhythmias and characteristic ECG findings (eg, delta waves), which are not seen in this patient.

Educational Objective: The most likely diagnosis in this patient, who has sudden onset of a severe headache and meningeal signs (nuchal rigidity), is subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH). Associated cranial nerve deficits, particularly involving the oculomotor nerve, may indicate the presence or rupture of an aneurysm. Evaluation: SAH classically presents with an abrupt, severe headache (often described as “the worst headache of life”) that frequently onsets during exertion and is often associated with neck stiffness, vomiting, and depressed mental status. Evaluation begins with emergent noncontrast CT scan of the head, followed by lumbar puncture if CT scan is negative but suspicion remains high. Definition: SAH refers to bleeding into the subarachnoid space, commonly due to rupture of a saccular aneurysm at the circle of Willis. Blood in the subarachnoid space causes meningeal irritation and leads to nuchal rigidity and photophobia. Increased intracranial pressure and irritation of cranial nerves, especially the oculomotor nerve, can cause coma, anisocoria, and ophthalmoplegia. SAH is life-threatening and requires immediate diagnosis and management. Prevention: Prevention of SAH includes managing risk factors for the development of aneurysms, such as preventing head trauma. Risk factors for aneurysm formation and rupture include hypertension and smoking. Treatment: Management includes blood pressure control, nimodipine to prevent vasospasm, and definitive aneurysm repair via surgical clipping or endovascular coiling. Seizure prophylaxis is appropriate. Supportive care in an intensive care setting is essential. Differential: In this patient with sudden and severe headache during exercise, nuchal rigidity, oculomotor nerve dysfunction, and hypertension, SAH is the most likely diagnosis. The acute onset and meningeal signs distinguish SAH from other causes of headache or focal deficits. Incorrect Answers: A, B, C, D, and F. Choice A: Acute cerebral infarction is incorrect. Acute cerebral infarction (ischemic stroke) typically presents with focal neurologic deficits without a sudden severe headache or meningeal signs like nuchal rigidity. Strokes are generally painless. Choice B: Arteriovenous malformation is incorrect. Although arteriovenous malformations can bleed, they are less likely to present with a thunderclap headache and meningeal irritation. Arteriovenous malformation, when ruptured, presents with altered mental status, headache, and focal neurologic deficits based on the cerebral territory affected. Epidural hematoma typically follows head or maxillofacial trauma and classically presents with loss of consciousness, followed by a lucid interval, followed by rapid worsening of headache, cranial nerve deficits, stupor or coma, and signs of herniation. Epidural hematoma would not likely present as a spontaneous headache during exercise. Choice F: Subdural hematoma is incorrect. Subdural hematoma usually presents slowly over hours to days, especially in older adults or after trauma, and does not typically cause a sudden thunderclap headache with meningeal signs.
